analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies on profits above $40 a barrel for one year and cuts the federal gas tax by 10 cents a gallon.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote, after being introduced by Rep. Menendez with 6 Democratic cosponsors in September 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2005 gas price spike, this bill would have imposed a one-year 50% excise tax on oil companies' profits from every barrel of crude oil sold above $40, and used the money for highways. At the same time, it would have cut the federal gasoline tax by 10 cents per gallon for one year, with the Highway Trust Fund made whole from the windfall tax receipts and, if needed, the general fund. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and other consumers of gasoline, who would pay 10 cents a gallon less in federal fuel tax for one year. Highway funding would be protected: windfall tax receipts would flow to the Highway Trust Fund, and any shortfall from the gas tax cut would be backfilled from the general fund. Renewable energy producers could also benefit indirectly, because oil companies could reduce the windfall tax by making qualified investments in facilities like renewable electricity projects.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the federal excise tax on highway motor fuels by 10 cents per gallon for the one-year period beginning on enactment.
Imposes a 50% excise tax on integrated oil companies' windfall profit — the amount by which the sale price of a barrel of crude oil exceeds a $40 base price — for one year.
Directs windfall profit tax receipts to the Highway Trust Fund and appropriates general fund money so the gas tax reduction does not leave the fund short.
Refunds dealers the tax already paid on fuel still in inventory when the rate drops, and exempts small holdings (under 2,000 gallons) from the tax when rates are restored.

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies, which would pay 50% of the windfall profit on every barrel above $40 for one year (though they could deduct the tax and offset it with qualified investments). If windfall receipts did not cover the cost of the gas tax cut, the general fund — taxpayers broadly — would cover the difference. Some of the windfall tax could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows companies to deduct the windfall profit tax from income taxes and to reduce it through qualified investments, which softens the tax's bite.

Part of the windfall tax could be passed through to consumers in higher prices, and the economic literature on the 1980 windfall profits tax found it discouraged domestic oil production and increased imports — a cost honest supporters would have to acknowledge.
The gas tax cut is funded partly by general fund appropriations, meaning all federal taxpayers backfill highway revenue if windfall tax receipts fall short of the cut's cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers, a 10-cent-per-gallon cut is modest but real relief during a price spike, paid for by a tax on oil profits above $40 a barrel. The design is imperfect: the deductibility of the tax and the investment offset blunt it, and a windfall profits tax risks some reduction in domestic production, as the 1980s version did. On balance the bill's costs fall mostly on large oil companies and the benefits fall on consumers, though the general fund backfill spreads some cost to all taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Menendez introduced the Gas Price Relief Act of 2005 on September 13, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Six House Democrats cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further action: no committee hearing or markup was held and no vote ever occurred before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies are better off because the bill died, since they avoided a 50% tax on profits above $40 per barrel. Drivers received none of the proposed 10-cent-per-gallon relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies and the committee that buried it

for.name: Rep. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would tax oil company windfall profits and cut the federal gas tax by 10 cents a gallon.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats; the bill then sat untouched in the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee with no Republican support on record.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 50% of their profits above $40 per barrel for one year, though they could deduct the tax and offset it with qualified investments. Their interest in stopping it ran directly against the gas price relief offered to consumers.
Dealers would be refunded tax paid on fuel in inventory when the rate dropped, but would owe a floor stocks tax when the rate was restored, with small holdings under 2,000 gallons exempt.

industries.industry: Renewable energy facilities (e.g. wind, solar, geothermal projects)
industries.note: Oil companies could reduce the windfall tax by making qualified investments in facilities described in section 45, creating a one-year incentive to invest in renewable energy.
